_note: One mystery a week for thirty-six weeks at every grade that has been written. Each case is a short story, a question, the suspects with what the text says about each, and the teacher answer with its proof quotes. A mystery is a claim-and-evidence task in disguise, which is why it sits beside the writing step and uses the same frame. cases.title: The Case of the Volcano That Would Not Erupt
cases.story: Four model volcanoes erupted at the fair and the fifth only fizzed. All five used two spoons of baking soda and half a cup of vinegar. The soda and the vinegar came from the same two containers. Baking soda and vinegar make gas, and the gas is what pushes the foam up. Baking soda left open to damp air slowly reacts and loses its power. The fifth team's soda had sat open on a humid porch since September. Its surface was crusted and clumped rather than loose and powdery. The fifth cone was built to the same height and the same opening. The vinegar in the fifth cup still smelled as sharp as the rest.
cases.question: Why did the fifth volcano only fizz?

suspects.who: 🥄 Baking soda spoiled by damp air
suspects.why: its surface was crusted and clumped
the vinegar still smelled as sharp as the rest
built to the same height and the same opening
all five used two spoons and half a cup

cases.answer: The fifth team's baking soda had already reacted in damp air.
proof: “Baking soda left open to damp air slowly reacts and loses its power.”
“The fifth team's soda had sat open on a humid porch since September.”
clears: Weak vinegar: “The vinegar in the fifth cup still smelled as sharp as the rest.”
A badly built cone: “The fifth cone was built to the same height and the same opening.”
Wrong amounts: “All five used two spoons of baking soda and half a cup of vinegar.”
cases.explain: Same recipe, same cone, same vinegar. Because soda left open in damp air spends its power before it ever reaches the cup, two spoons of crusted soda cannot make the gas that four spoons of fresh soda made.

cases.title: The Case of the Crown That Would Not Close
cases.story: Twenty paper crowns were cut to one pattern and six would not close. The six that failed were all cut by the same two students. A circle's distance around is a little more than three times its width. The six short crowns each measure close to a third of what they need. The other fourteen students measured around with a tape as instructed.

suspects.why: the distance around is a little more than three times the width
nobody trimmed, tore or re-cut any crown
every crown came off the same roll at the same width
twenty crowns were cut to one pattern

“The six short crowns each measure close to a third of what they need.”

A narrower roll: “Every crown came off the same roll of card at the same width.”
A different pattern: “Twenty paper crowns were cut to one pattern and six would not close.”

cases.title: The Case of the Piano That Went Sour
cases.story: The music room piano was tuned in October and sounded wrong by February. No other instrument in the building had shifted at all. Nobody had moved the piano and no string had broken. A piano string is stretched across a wooden frame that holds its tension. Wood takes in water from damp air and gives it up in dry air, swelling and shrinking as it does. A frame that shrinks lets every string go slightly slack at once. The music room humidity ran at fifty-five percent in October and nineteen in February. The other instruments live in cases that hold their own air. The tuner found every string flat by about the same amount.
cases.question: Why did the piano go out of tune?

suspects.who: 💨 Dry winter air shrinking the frame
suspects.why: a frame that shrinks lets every string go slack at once
nobody had moved the piano

suspects.who: 🎻 A problem in the whole building
suspects.why: no other instrument had shifted at all
no string had broken

cases.answer: Dry February air shrank the wooden frame and loosened every string.
proof: “A frame that shrinks lets every string go slightly slack at once.”
“The music room humidity ran at fifty-five percent in October and nineteen in February.”
clears: The piano being moved: “Nobody had moved the piano and no string had broken.”
The whole building: “No other instrument in the building had shifted at all.”
A broken string: “no string had broken.”
cases.explain: Every string went flat by the same amount, which no single broken string can do. Because the humidity fell from fifty-five percent to nineteen, the frame holding all of them shrank and let the whole set go slack together.

cases.title: The Case of the Kite That Would Not Climb
cases.story: Two identical kites flew on the same afternoon and only one would climb. Both were built from the same kit with the same tail and string. The flag on the roof stood straight out all afternoon. A kite climbs on air that moves steadily in one direction. A building sends the wind over its roof and leaves a churning pocket behind it. The one that climbed was flown in the open field beyond the gym. A ribbon held up on the lawn flapped in every direction at once.
cases.question: Why would one kite not climb?

suspects.why: a ribbon on the lawn flapped in every direction at once
the flag on the roof stood straight out all afternoon
both were built from the same kit
the same tail and string on both

cases.answer: The gym churned the wind on the lawn so the kite had no steady air.
proof: “A building sends the wind over its roof and leaves a churning pocket behind it.”
“That pocket pushes up, down and sideways by turns instead of steadily.”
clears: No wind: “The flag on the roof stood straight out all afternoon.”
A badly built kite: “Both were built from the same kit with the same tail and string.”
The tail: “Both were built from the same kit with the same tail and string.”
cases.explain: There was plenty of wind and two identical kites. Because the gym leaves a churning pocket behind it, the kite on the lawn was pushed four ways at once while the one in the open field had steady air to climb on.

cases.title: The Case of the Shamrock That Closed at Four
cases.story: The shamrock plant on the sill folded its leaves shut every afternoon at four. It opened again each morning without anyone touching it. The soil stayed evenly damp and the plant never wilted. No insect, mold or damage was found on any leaf. Some plants fold their leaves on a daily rhythm set by light. The folding happens on schedule whether or not the plant is short of water. A storage shed built in January now blocks the sill from three o'clock on. Before January the sill held direct light until nearly seven. A second shamrock in the sunnier window folds at close to seven instead.
cases.question: Why does the shamrock close at four?

suspects.why: some plants fold their leaves on a rhythm set by light
the soil stayed evenly damp and the plant never wilted
no insect, mold or damage was found on any leaf
it opened again each morning without anyone touching it

cases.answer: The new shed cuts the light that sets the plant's folding rhythm.
proof: “Some plants fold their leaves on a daily rhythm set by light.”
“A storage shed built in January now blocks the sill from three o'clock on.”
clears: Dry soil: “The soil stayed evenly damp and the plant never wilted.”
Pests or disease: “No insect, mold or damage was found on any leaf.”
Somebody touching it: “It opened again each morning without anyone touching it.”
cases.explain: The second shamrock is the control. Because the sunnier window still holds light until seven and folds at seven, the plant on the shaded sill is reading the shed, not thirst or damage.

cases.title: The Case of the Puddle That Stayed
cases.story: One puddle on the field lasted nine days and every other puddle dried in two. All of them filled during the same Saturday rain. The long puddle sits in a shallow dip only two inches deep. Water leaves the ground by soaking down or drying off the top. Soil made of fine packed clay lets water through many times more slowly than sandy soil. A core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay. Samples from the other spots came up brown and sandy. Sun and wind reached every part of the field equally all nine days. The dip is not fed by any pipe, downspout or stream.
cases.question: Why did one puddle last nine days?

suspects.why: a core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay
the dip is only two inches deep
the dip is not fed by any pipe, downspout or stream
sun and wind reached every part of the field equally

cases.answer: Clay soil under the dip let the water soak down very slowly.
proof: “Soil made of fine packed clay lets water through many times more slowly than sandy soil.”
“A core sample from the dip came up as grey packed clay.”
clears: A deeper hole: “The long puddle sits in a shallow dip only two inches deep.”
Water feeding in: “The dip is not fed by any pipe, downspout or stream.”
Less sun: “Sun and wind reached every part of the field equally all nine days.”
cases.explain: It is the shallowest puddle and it lasted longest, so depth is not the answer. Because the soil under it is packed clay while the rest of the field is sandy, the water had almost no way down.

cases.title: The Case of the Seeds That Never Came Up
cases.story: Two rows of sunflower seeds went in on the same morning and one row sprouted. Both rows came from the same packet, dated this year. Both were watered by the same hose on the same schedule. A seed carries only enough stored food to push a shoot a short way up. A seed buried too deep runs out of food before the shoot reaches light. The sprouting row was planted half an inch down as the packet says. The second row was planted four inches down with a trowel. Dug up three weeks later, the deep seeds had sprouted and then died underground. The soil in both rows was the same loose mix at the same warmth.
cases.question: Why did one row never come up?

suspects.why: a seed buried too deep runs out of food before reaching light
the deep seeds had sprouted and then died underground
both were watered by the same hose on the same schedule
the soil in both rows was the same loose mix at the same warmth

cases.answer: The deep row sprouted underground and ran out of food before surfacing.
proof: “A seed buried too deep runs out of food before the shoot reaches light.”
“The second row was planted four inches down with a trowel.”
clears: Dead seed: “Dug up three weeks later, the deep seeds had sprouted and then died underground.”
Too little water: “Both were watered by the same hose on the same schedule.”
Cold soil: “The soil in both rows was the same loose mix at the same warmth.”
cases.explain: The seeds were alive — they germinated. Because four inches is further than a sunflower's stored food can push a shoot, the row sprouted and then starved before it ever reached the surface.

cases.title: The Case of the Egg That Floated
cases.story: Six eggs went into a bowl of water and one floated while five sank. All six came from the same farm and the same carton. None of them was cracked, warm or smelling of anything. An egg has a small air pocket at its blunt end just inside the shell. The shell is slightly porous, so water leaves the egg slowly and air takes its place. The longer an egg is kept, the larger that air pocket grows. An egg floats once its air pocket is large enough to lift it. Marcus found a second date stamp on the floating egg reading five weeks earlier. The five sinking eggs all carried this week's stamp.
cases.question: Why did one egg float?

suspects.who: 🫧 A grown air pocket in an older egg
suspects.why: an egg floats once its air pocket is large enough
none of them was cracked
all six came from the same farm and the same carton
none of them was warm

cases.answer: The floating egg was five weeks older and its air pocket had grown.
proof: “The longer an egg is kept, the larger that air pocket grows.”
“Marcus found a second date stamp on the floating egg reading five weeks earlier.”
clears: A cracked shell: “None of them was cracked, warm or smelling of anything.”
A different farm: “All six came from the same farm and the same carton.”
Being warm: “None of them was cracked, warm or smelling of anything.”
cases.explain: One carton, one farm, five weeks of difference. Because water leaves an egg slowly and air replaces it, the oldest egg carries the biggest air pocket, and that is what lifted it off the bottom.

cases.title: The Case of the Shadow That Moved House

the pole's height was measured both times at twenty-nine feet

suspects.why: a sprinter covers about seven feet in that time
the camera sat locked on a tripod
the focus ring was taped in place before the meet
the lens was clean

cases.title: The Case of the Leaning Bean Plant
cases.story: A bean plant on the counter leaned hard toward the window by Friday. It had stood straight on Monday and nobody had tipped the pot. cases.question: Why did the bean plant lean?

the soil was level and the pot sat flat on the counter
the stem was firm and green with no sign of rot
both plants had the same soil, water and pot

proof: “A plant grows the cells on its shaded side longer than those on its lit side.”
“The window is the room's only light source and sits to the plant's left.”

Uneven watering: “Both plants had the same soil, water and pot.”

cases.title: The Case of the Ice Cream in the Metal Bowl

neither bowl was in sunlight
both bowls had been sitting at seventy-one degrees all morning
both scoops were the same size from the same tub

proof: “Heat moves into ice cream from whatever is touching it.”
“Metal carries heat many times faster than plastic does.”

cases.title: The Case of the Balloons That Sank Overnight
cases.story: Thirty foil balloons touched the gym ceiling on Friday and rested on the floor on Monday. None of them had popped and every knot still held. Foil holds helium far better than latex and these were all foil. A gas shrinks when it cools and takes up less room than it did warm. A balloon floats only while it pushes aside more air than it weighs. A balloon that shrinks pushes aside less air and stops floating. The gym heat is switched off from Friday evening until Monday morning. A logger in the gym recorded sixty-eight degrees Friday and forty-one on Sunday. Every balloon measured smaller around on Monday than it had on Friday.
cases.question: Why did the balloons sink?

suspects.who: 🌡️ The cold gym shrinking the gas
suspects.why: a balloon that shrinks pushes aside less air and stops floating
foil holds helium far better than latex and these were all foil
none of them had popped and every knot still held
every balloon measured smaller around on Monday

cases.answer: The cold weekend gym shrank the helium until the balloons sank.
proof: “A logger in the gym recorded sixty-eight degrees Friday and forty-one on Sunday.”
“Every balloon measured smaller around on Monday than it had on Friday.”
clears: Helium leaking: “Foil holds helium far better than latex and these were all foil.”
A leak or a pop: “None of them had popped and every knot still held.”
Heavier ribbons: “Every balloon measured smaller around on Monday than it had on Friday.”
cases.explain: The measurement is the proof: they are smaller, not emptier. Because the heat went off and the gym fell to forty-one degrees, the helium shrank, each balloon pushed aside less air, and thirty of them stopped floating at once.
